title: Effects of virtual reality-based rehabilitation on upper-limb motor function and functional independence after subacute stroke: A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
content:
by Joaquín Pérez-Cárcamo, Edgar Vásquez-Carrasco, Pablo Valdés-Badilla, Cristian Sandoval-Vásquez, Cristian Núñez-Espinosa, Jordan Hernandez-Martínez

Background

Virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation has emerged as a promising approach to enhance recovery after stroke; however, its effectiveness during the subacute phase remains unclear. This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis evaluated the effects of VR-based rehabilitation on upper-limb motor function, manual dexterity, and functional independence in individuals with subacute stroke.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL Complete, and Psychology and Behavioral Sciences Collection were searched through May 2026. Randomized controlled trials involving adults with subacute stroke receiving immersive or non-immersive VR-based rehabilitation were included. Comparators consisted of active or inactive control interventions. Methodological quality was assessed using TESTEX, risk of bias using RoB 2, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. A multilevel meta-analysis was conducted to account for dependency among multiple effect sizes.

Results

Eleven randomized controlled trials involving 510 unique participants met the inclusion criteria. VR-based rehabilitation significantly improved upper-limb motor function, based on pooled Fugl-Meyer Assessment–Upper Extremity and Action Research Arm Test outcomes (Hedges’ g = 0.56, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.98, p = 0.009). Functional independence, assessed using Barthel-type scales and Functional Independence Measure outcomes, also showed significant improvements favoring VR-based rehabilitation (Hedges’ g = 0.45, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.79, p = 0.007). The pooled effect for manual dexterity, assessed using the Box and Block Test, favored VR-based rehabilitation but was not statistically significant (Hedges’ g = 0.47, 95% CI −0.40 to 1.34, p = 0.285).

Conclusions

VR-based rehabilitation may enhance upper-limb motor recovery and functional independence in individuals with subacute stroke. However, evidence for manual dexterity remains inconclusive. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials with standardized intervention protocols and outcome measures are needed to clarify the broader functional effects of VR-based rehabilitation during the subacute phase of stroke recovery.
author: Joaquín Pérez-Cárcamo
